posts.title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone
posts.subtitle: Belonging, friendship, and the first step into an unfamiliar world.
posts.author: J. K. Rowling
posts.intro: Harry grows up unwanted in the Dursleys’ home until an invitation to Hogwarts reveals that he is a wizard. School brings friendship with Ron and Hermione, a connection to his parents, and a mystery involving an object hidden inside the castle.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

The adventure begins as an escape from loneliness but becomes a story about belonging through choices. Harry’s new world is exciting and imperfect: prejudice, rivalry, and danger exist alongside wonder. The friendship at its centre depends on different strengths, rather than one person being able to do everything.

## A question to carry away

How does a place become a home? The book suggests that friendship and everyday acts of courage are as important as extraordinary abilities.
posts.ending: Harry, Ron, and Hermione follow clues to the protected Philosopher’s Stone. Harry discovers that Professor Quirrell, who carries Voldemort, is trying to steal it. Harry prevents the theft; the Stone is later destroyed. His mother’s protection matters more than the power Voldemort wants.

posts.title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
posts.subtitle: A mystery about prejudice, identity, and the danger of inherited beliefs.
posts.author: J. K. Rowling
posts.intro: Harry’s second year at Hogwarts is unsettled by attacks that leave students petrified. Rumours about the Chamber of Secrets turn suspicion toward Harry, especially when others discover he can speak to snakes. A mysterious diary offers a misleading account of the past.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

The school’s history becomes a weapon when ideas about blood status determine who is considered worthy. Harry also fears that a resemblance to Voldemort means he is destined to become like him. The novel separates a person’s abilities from the decisions that give those abilities meaning.

## A question to carry away

Who benefits when people accept an old prejudice without questioning it? This story makes that question part of a school mystery.
posts.ending: The diary contains a young Tom Riddle, who has manipulated Ginny Weasley into opening the Chamber. Harry faces its basilisk, saves Ginny, and destroys the diary with a basilisk fang. He also helps free Dobby from the Malfoys.

posts.title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
posts.subtitle: Fear, misleading stories, and the possibility of finding family.
posts.author: J. K. Rowling
posts.intro: Sirius Black escapes Azkaban, and Harry is told that the fugitive threatens his life. Dementors guard Hogwarts, forcing Harry to confront memories of his parents’ deaths. Professor Lupin teaches him a different way to respond to fear.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

The novel asks how much of a person’s reputation rests on a story that was never properly tested. New information changes Harry’s understanding of his family and the people around him. Its treatment of fear is equally important: strength can grow from memory, practice, and support.

## A question to carry away

What changes when we hear a second version of an event? This is the series’ clearest early lesson in revising a confident judgment.
posts.ending: Sirius is revealed to be Harry’s godfather, wrongly blamed for the betrayal committed by Peter Pettigrew. Pettigrew escapes. Harry and Hermione use a Time-Turner to save Buckbeak and help Sirius flee, though Harry cannot yet move in with him.

posts.title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire
posts.subtitle: Competition turns into a confrontation with a danger the world has underestimated.
posts.author: J. K. Rowling
posts.intro: Hogwarts hosts the Triwizard Tournament, and Harry is unexpectedly selected as a fourth champion. He faces dangerous tasks while trying to understand who entered his name. The widening world of magical schools and international competition gives the year an uneasy excitement.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

The tournament rewards skill, but its deeper test is judgment. Harry must decide when to compete, when to help, and whom to trust. The spectacle around the event also shows how easily an audience can miss a threat unfolding in plain sight.

## A question to carry away

What does doing the right thing mean inside a competition? The ending also changes the series from school adventures into a story shaped by loss.
posts.ending: Harry and Cedric reach the final trophy together. It transports them to a graveyard, where Cedric is killed and Voldemort regains a body. Harry escapes. The supposed Moody is exposed as Barty Crouch Jr., who arranged Harry’s path through the tournament.

posts.title: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix
posts.subtitle: Resistance, grief, and learning to act when authority refuses to listen.
posts.author: J. K. Rowling
posts.intro: After Voldemort’s return, the Ministry denies the threat and undermines Harry’s account. Dolores Umbridge takes control at Hogwarts, restricting meaningful defence lessons. Harry and his friends form Dumbledore’s Army to learn what the official classroom will not teach.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

The book examines institutions that protect their own image instead of the people they serve. Harry’s anger and isolation complicate his relationships, while the students’ shared practice creates a practical form of resistance. Knowledge becomes something they build together.

## A question to carry away

When is obedience a virtue, and when does it become avoidance? The novel gives collective learning an unusually strong role in answering that question.
posts.ending: Voldemort uses a false vision to lure Harry to the Department of Mysteries. During the resulting battle, Sirius dies. Voldemort is finally seen by Ministry officials, making denial impossible. Dumbledore explains the prophecy linking Harry and Voldemort.

posts.title: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince
posts.subtitle: The past becomes a map of the conflict still to come.
posts.author: J. K. Rowling
posts.intro: Dumbledore guides Harry through memories of Voldemort’s earlier life. Meanwhile, Harry finds a used Potions textbook filled with helpful notes and dangerous spells. Draco’s secret work and the book’s unknown owner turn a familiar school year into a period of growing uncertainty.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

The story connects the desire for control with the refusal to accept mortality. It also questions the attraction of shortcuts: information can be useful without its source being trustworthy. Harry’s success with the textbook becomes inseparable from his responsibility for what he learns.

## A question to carry away

Can we separate a useful discovery from the character of its maker? The book leaves Harry facing a task he can no longer hand to a mentor.
posts.ending: Harry and Dumbledore investigate Horcruxes, objects holding fragments of Voldemort’s soul. A mission to retrieve one leaves Dumbledore weakened. Back at Hogwarts, Snape kills him and is revealed as the Half-Blood Prince. The recovered locket proves to be a substitute.

posts.title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows
posts.subtitle: The final choice between domination and the courage to accept loss.
posts.author: J. K. Rowling
posts.intro: Harry, Ron, and Hermione leave school to search for Voldemort’s remaining Horcruxes. Without the routines and protection of Hogwarts, friendship is tested by fear, uncertainty, and exhaustion. The legend of the Deathly Hallows offers another possible route to power.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

The final novel measures courage through the willingness to continue without certainty. Loyalty must survive disappointment, and heroism depends on many people whose work is less visible than Harry’s. The contrast between Horcruxes and Hallows brings the fear of death to the centre of the story.

## A question to carry away

What kind of power is worth having? The series ends by giving love, restraint, and the acceptance of mortality more weight than invulnerability.
posts.ending: The Horcruxes are destroyed, and Snape’s memories reveal his hidden loyalty and the truth about Harry’s connection to Voldemort. Harry willingly faces death and survives. At Hogwarts, Voldemort falls when the Elder Wand’s allegiance defeats his assumptions. An epilogue shows the next generation heading to school.

posts.title: The Sun Is Also a Star
posts.subtitle: One day in New York, two lives, and the tension between chance and choice.
posts.author: Nicola Yoon
posts.intro: Natasha, a Jamaican teenager, is trying to prevent her family’s deportation. Daniel, a Korean American teenager, is heading toward a future his parents have planned for him. They meet in New York and spend a day arguing about science, poetry, and whether love can arrive so quickly.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

Their different ways of seeing the world make the romance a conversation rather than a simple agreement. Brief shifts toward other lives show how strangers can influence one another without realising it. Immigration and family expectations give their limited time together real stakes.

## A question to carry away

How much of a life comes from chance, and how much from what we do with it? The novel holds both ideas together without resolving the tension.
posts.ending: The family’s deportation goes ahead, and Natasha and Daniel’s relationship does not withstand the distance. Years later, a chance reunion on a plane opens the possibility of another beginning.

posts.title: Everything, Everything
posts.subtitle: A sheltered life opens into questions about freedom, trust, and risk.
posts.author: Nicola Yoon
posts.intro: Madeline Whittier has grown up inside her home believing that a severe immune disorder makes the outside world dangerous. Her mother and nurse organise a carefully controlled life. When Olly moves in next door, their messages become a relationship that makes her imagine a different future.
posts.body:
## The ideas beneath the story

The romance opens a larger question about who gets to define safety. The story’s short chapters, messages, and illustrations mirror Maddy’s attempt to assemble a life beyond the limits she has been given.

## A question to carry away

When can care become control? This is a fictional story about autonomy and family, rather than medical guidance about immune disorders.
posts.ending: After an unauthorised trip and a medical crisis, Maddy learns that the diagnosis shaping her life was false. Her mother’s grief and fear have sustained the confinement. Maddy begins to reclaim her independence and reconnects with Olly.

posts.title: London and the art of noticing.
posts.subtitle: A visual notebook of open skies, winter paths, and quiet moments.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: A travel gallery does not have to be a list of landmarks. Sometimes a patch of grass, a bare branch, or the surface of a lake carries more of a place’s atmosphere than a famous silhouette. The London photographs in this collection make room for those smaller details.
posts.body:
## Look beyond the obvious

A city offers more than one pace. A road organizes movement; a park creates room to pause. In the photograph of the open field, the sky occupies much of the frame while people share a small part of the ground. That balance gives the ordinary scene a feeling of space.

There is no need to turn every image into a claim about the city as a whole. A photograph is a selected view, made at a particular moment. It can preserve something worthwhile without standing in for every possible experience of London.

> A place becomes more memorable when we give its ordinary details some attention.

## Let the seasons remain visible

The winter path has a different rhythm. Bare branches spread across the frame, while scattered snow and the long line of the path lead the eye into the distance. Its interest comes from the contrast between delicate marks and a clear direction.

At the lake, the quieter tones make a different kind of picture. The water, sky, and distant trees share a restrained palette. Keeping those differences lets the collection feel like a set of moments, rather than making every photograph look as if it were taken at the same time.

## Edit for coherence

A consistent treatment helps a gallery hold together. Controlled highlights, gentle shadow detail, and natural colors can make moving between photographs more comfortable. The aim is a shared balance, while allowing a sunny field and a winter view to remain recognizably different.

These images have been edited for the blog’s gallery. Their captions identify the subjects without adding an invented travel diary, precise date, or unverified story about what happened outside the frame. The pictures can carry their own part of the notebook.

## Keep a visual notebook

A visual notebook can be as simple as a photograph and one sentence about what caught your attention. The sentence helps explain the choice; the photograph preserves details that language may miss. Together they offer a reason to look again.

The gallery collects photographs from my December 2025 London trip. It connects places with the subjects explored elsewhere on the blog: learning, reading, building, and the pleasure of paying attention.

![A winter path · London collection supplied by Ahmad; edited for this gallery.](assets/images/london-winter-1600.webp)

posts.title: Reading beyond the summary.
posts.subtitle: What an outline can preserve—and what it leaves for the book itself.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: A summary is a useful doorway into a book. It can help us remember a plot, compare themes, or decide what to read next. It also leaves things outside the doorway: rhythm, atmosphere, the slow change of a character, and the experience of discovering something in the author’s chosen order.
posts.body:
## Keep the layers separate

The plot tells us what happens. The themes suggest what the story might be asking. A personal response describes what a reader brings to it. Keeping those layers separate makes a reading note clearer and leaves room for someone else to respond differently.

The distinction matters for fiction especially. A concise account of an event can be accurate without capturing its emotional weight. A thematic interpretation can be interesting without being the only reading available. A useful summary is confident about the facts and open about the interpretation.

> A summary can keep the outline. Reading gives the outline a life.

## Leave room for discovery

Knowing an ending changes the experience of reading toward it. Some readers want that information; others do not. Separating ending spoilers from the main summary gives both groups a choice and keeps a reading note useful before and after the book.

There is no need to make every summary comprehensive. Sometimes the right purpose is to preserve a central conflict, identify a few questions, and point toward the full work. The note should make its scope clear instead of pretending to contain everything a book offers.

## Carry a question away

A good reading note can end with a question rather than a verdict. What makes a place feel like home? Which choices reveal a character more clearly than their abilities? When does protection become restriction? Questions create a bridge between the story and later reflection.

That bridge is one reason fiction can remain interesting long after its plot is familiar. Returning to a story with a different question can reveal a detail that mattered less the first time. The book remains the same, while the reader’s attention changes.

## Return to the pages

The summaries on this blog are companions to the books. They use original wording to record an outline and a few ideas, with the ending marked separately. The real covers identify the editions being discussed, and the full stories remain worth reading in their own words.

A note becomes more valuable when it sends us back to the source with sharper attention. It is a place to keep a thought, then a reason to continue exploring beyond it.

posts.title: Build something small and useful.
posts.subtitle: The first version should answer a real question.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: An idea often becomes more exciting as its feature list grows. It becomes more useful when its purpose becomes clearer. A small first version can create a better conversation with the people it is meant to help, because it makes the central promise visible.
posts.body:
## Start with a moment

Describe the situation in which someone needs help. What are they trying to finish? What is awkward about the current process? What result would make their day easier? A concrete moment gives the product a sharper purpose than a broad ambition to improve everything.

A tool for keeping reading notes, for example, might begin with one need: remember an idea and find it again. It does not immediately need a social network, a marketplace, or an elaborate recommendation system. The smallest useful version should make the core action work well.

> A small useful thing is a better question than a large vague promise.

## Keep the promise testable

A first version can test whether the problem is real, whether the proposed workflow is understandable, and whether someone comes back after trying it. Those are different questions. Counting a first visit alone cannot answer all of them.

The test should be honest about what it measures. A conversation can reveal confusion, a prototype can reveal usability problems, and repeated use can suggest continuing value. None is a guarantee of a successful business, but each can reduce a specific uncertainty.

## Spend effort where it changes the result

Polish is valuable when it makes a useful thing reliable and clear. It is less valuable when it hides an unresolved purpose behind attractive screens. Early effort should make the main task work, explain its limits, and make failures understandable.

That does not require a careless first version. A small scope can make quality easier to achieve. Fewer features leave more time for the words, interactions, and details that the first users actually encounter.

## Let evidence change the plan

Building includes the willingness to discover that an assumption was wrong. A feature may be unnecessary, an expected audience may use the tool differently, or a simple workflow may be more valuable than the original plan. That information is part of progress.

A useful next step is often to improve one thing that someone genuinely needs. The product grows around evidence instead of around an ever-expanding list of possibilities. Small beginnings leave room for better judgment.

posts.title: A good interface respects attention.
posts.subtitle: Clear choices, quiet details, and the craft of making software feel simple.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: An interface is a conversation made of labels, controls, and feedback. Every unclear button asks the visitor to do extra interpretation. Every useful detail gives some of that attention back. Good design begins by deciding what a person has come to do.
posts.body:
## Choose a main task

A page can contain many things while still having one clear purpose. An article page should make reading comfortable. A contact page should make sending a message straightforward. A dashboard should help its owner understand what needs attention and where to act.

When every element demands emphasis, emphasis loses its meaning. A visual hierarchy gives the main task room, then makes supporting choices available without turning them into competing headlines. Simplicity comes from making those decisions, rather than merely removing decoration.

> Clarity is a way of respecting someone else’s time.

## Use words that help

A label should describe what happens next. Save draft and Publish describe different actions, and that difference matters. A good confirmation says what was saved and whether it is visible to others. An error explains what needs changing instead of simply announcing failure.

The same principle belongs in navigation. A visitor should not need to learn a private naming system to find articles, books, or contact information. Familiar words create a useful foundation; personality can come through the writing and visual details around them.

## Design for different ways of using it

People use different screens, keyboards, pointing devices, and motion preferences. A control that works only on hover leaves some visitors without the same information. A visible focus indicator and a readable label make the path through a page easier to follow.

Responsive design is more than shrinking a desktop layout. Long headings need room, tap targets need space, and multi-column arrangements sometimes need a different order. The task should remain clear when the available space changes.

## Let polish serve the purpose

A rounded panel, a careful type scale, or a gentle transition can make a page feel considered. Those details work best when they help separate content, reveal an action, or keep the page comfortable to use. Animation should have a reason to exist and a quiet way to stop.

The final question is practical: can someone understand what is here and do what they came to do? A polished interface answers that question through many small decisions that fit together.

posts.title: AI and the habit of questioning.
posts.subtitle: Useful tools still need a thoughtful person on the other side.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: A tool that produces an answer quickly can be helpful. It can also make it easier to move past a question before understanding it. The useful challenge is to keep the speed while preserving the habits that make learning reliable: checking, comparing, and explaining.
posts.body:
## Give the task a shape

A vague request often produces a vague result. A more useful request names the goal, the audience, the available information, and the form an answer should take. Asking for three alternative explanations can be more productive than asking for the final truth in one paragraph.

This is partly a lesson in thinking clearly. Before handing a problem to a tool, we have to decide what the problem is. That decision is valuable even when the tool is never used. A precise question gives both the person and the system a better place to start.

> A helpful answer should make the next question clearer.

## Keep a way to check

For a technical claim, return to a trusted primary source, a worked calculation, or a test that can be repeated. A plausible explanation is not the same thing as a verified one. The ability to produce smooth language does not remove the need for evidence.

In code, that might mean trying a small input, inspecting an error case, and checking what happens when an assumption fails. In study, it might mean solving a problem independently and comparing methods. The tool can support the work without becoming the only judge of it.

## Learn the mechanism

The phrase artificial intelligence can hide many different mechanisms. A simple neural-network introduction makes one family of models more concrete: inputs are transformed through weighted connections and nonlinear operations, and training adjusts parameters. That picture is useful without pretending it describes every current system.

The video below offers a visual starting point. It is an invitation to learn the mathematics behind a familiar term. Understanding even one mechanism carefully is often more valuable than collecting a long list of fashionable vocabulary.

## Stay responsible for the result

A useful tool can suggest a direction, reduce repetitive work, or offer a different explanation. Choosing what to keep remains a human decision. The person using an answer needs to know its limits and be able to explain why it deserves confidence.

That leaves room for curiosity and caution together. Explore the tool, ask better questions, and keep a method for checking what comes back. The result is a stronger learning process, with help available and judgment still engaged.

[youtube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aircAruvnKk)

posts.title: Understanding before formulas.
posts.subtitle: Why a sketch and a good question belong beside the equation.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: A formula can compress a great deal of understanding into a small space. That is its strength, but it can also make the understanding easy to skip. Learning becomes more satisfying when an equation is the end of an explanation we can follow, rather than the beginning of a procedure we can only repeat.
posts.body:
## Ask what is changing

Before choosing a formula, describe the situation in ordinary language. What changes with time? What stays approximately constant? What influences what? A rough sketch can reveal these relationships without requiring polished drawing or advanced notation.

For motion, a position graph and a velocity graph answer different questions. For a circuit, a voltage across a component and a current through it are different descriptions. Naming those differences makes it easier to choose the right mathematical tool.

> The equation is more useful when its symbols refer to something we can picture.

## Build an intuition, then test it

An intuitive explanation is a starting point, not a guarantee. It can help predict a direction of change or identify a relevant variable. The mathematics then tests that expectation more carefully and shows where an appealing picture may be incomplete.

Calculus is a good example of the conversation between pictures and symbols. A slope can describe local change, while accumulation brings small contributions together. Visual explanations can make those ideas approachable before formal rules make them precise.

## Explain it without hiding

Try explaining an equation to someone who has not seen it. Say what each quantity means, which assumptions are being made, and why the relationship is plausible. If the explanation breaks down, that is a useful place to return to the subject.

It also helps to create a small example and an edge case. A simple example makes the procedure concrete. An edge case asks whether the formula still behaves as expected when one quantity becomes unusually small or large.

## Give the ideas time

Understanding often arrives in stages. A topic that feels procedural on the first pass may become intuitive after a second explanation, a different diagram, or a problem that requires choosing the model independently. That change is part of learning, rather than evidence that the first effort was wasted.

The goal is to keep pictures, words, and equations connected. Each can expose something the others hide. Together they make a subject feel more coherent and give the next difficult question somewhere to begin.

[youtube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUvTyaaNkzM)

posts.title: The quiet power of checking units.
posts.subtitle: A small habit that can catch a large mistake.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: A page of algebra can look convincing while describing something impossible. One of the quickest ways to question it is to check the units. The habit is modest, almost unglamorous, but it keeps an answer attached to the physical quantity it claims to represent.
posts.body:
## Name the quantity

Distance, time, current, and energy are different kinds of quantities. A number by itself does not tell us which one we have found. Writing the unit beside a result forces that question into the open and makes the calculation more legible to someone else.

The same care belongs at the beginning. Write down the input units before substitution. A value in milliamperes and a value in amperes may describe the same kind of quantity, but using them without conversion can change a numerical answer by a thousand.

> A number becomes an answer only when we know what it measures.

## Make both sides agree

If an equation claims to calculate speed, its dimensions should reduce to length divided by time. If the units instead describe length multiplied by time, something needs attention. A missing division or an incorrect rearrangement may be easier to spot through units than through another pass at the algebra.

Consistency cannot prove that a formula is correct. A wrong dimensionless factor can pass a unit check. So can a relationship that uses the right dimensions but the wrong physics. The check is a filter, not a substitute for understanding.

## Try an extreme case

Unit checking becomes stronger when paired with a simple limiting case. What should happen when an input approaches zero? Does a result become unreasonably large when a resistance increases? Does a predicted time remain positive? These questions ask whether the mathematics still tells a sensible physical story.

A rough estimate is useful too. An order-of-magnitude expectation makes it harder for a misplaced decimal point to hide behind many digits. Precision is valuable after the result is plausible; it cannot rescue an implausible model.

## Use the habit outside physics

The idea applies to planning and building as well. Revenue is not profit, a monthly number is not an annual number, and users are not the same thing as visits. Naming what a number measures prevents unlike things from being compared as if they were interchangeable.

The practical routine is simple: label the inputs, track the units, check a limiting case, and explain the result in a sentence. It takes little space, but it can save a great deal of confusion.

posts.title: Seeing the world as waves.
posts.subtitle: Sound, signals, and a different way to notice what is happening around us.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: A sound is something we hear. A signal is something we measure. A wave gives us a way to connect those experiences to a changing pattern. Once the pattern becomes visible, a familiar world begins to look different: a note, a vibration, and an electrical trace become related questions.
posts.body:
## A pattern that travels

A wave is a disturbance that propagates. In a mechanical wave, the medium’s local motion and the movement of the disturbance are different things. Watching a ripple move across water can help separate those ideas: the visible pattern travels even though the water does not simply move across the pond with it.

Sound offers another entry point. Pressure changes travel through a medium, and the ear responds to those changes. Frequency describes how often a pattern repeats, while amplitude describes the size of a variation. These are different properties, and keeping them separate makes the description more useful.

> A complicated signal can become clearer when we ask which simpler patterns make it.

## One signal, many ingredients

A pure tone gives a relatively simple pattern. A musical instrument produces something richer. The Fourier perspective asks how a signal can be described through sinusoidal components of different frequencies. It gives us a vocabulary for the ingredients inside a complicated trace.

This does not mean every real-world signal repeats forever. The mathematical details depend on whether the signal is periodic, sampled, finite, or continuous. But the central question remains approachable: what changes when we look at this signal in terms of frequency rather than time?

## Pictures before procedures

An animation can make this change of viewpoint easier to understand. A moving curve gives the time view; a collection of frequency components gives another description of the same signal. Neither picture replaces the other. Each makes certain questions easier to ask.

The visual explanation below is a good starting point for that intuition. Watch for the role of rotation and averaging, then return to the equations. The animation is most useful when it leaves a question you can work through yourself.

## A new way of paying attention

A quiet room still contains patterns: distant traffic, a fan, a voice, a vibration through a table. Looking for those patterns can make signal processing feel less abstract. The subject begins with things we can notice before it reaches things we can calculate.

That is the appeal of waves as a way of thinking. They connect everyday experiences with a language that can describe them carefully, and they remind us that a useful explanation can change what we notice next.

[youtube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=spUNpyF58BY)

posts.title: What a circuit teaches about thinking.
posts.subtitle: Small systems, clear assumptions, and the value of a useful model.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: A circuit can look intimidating before it becomes understandable. Lines cross a page, symbols stand in for physical objects, and a few equations seem to hold the whole thing together. The first useful step is often a simple question: what is this system supposed to do? That question turns a collection of parts into a problem with a purpose.
posts.body:
## Begin with the boundary

Before calculating anything, decide what belongs inside the system. Is the source ideal? Are the connecting wires treated as having negligible resistance? Which voltage is measured relative to which reference? These decisions can look like minor housekeeping, but they determine what an answer actually means.

For an ideal resistor, Ohm’s law relates voltage, current, and resistance. It is a compact relationship, but it is useful within a model. Real components have limits, tolerances, and temperature effects. A calculation becomes stronger when its assumptions are written beside it rather than hidden beneath it.

> A useful model makes a difficult question small enough to work on.

## Predict before measuring

Consider a simple series circuit containing a source and two resistors. Before reaching for numbers, predict what should happen if one resistance increases. The current should decrease for the same ideal source voltage. That qualitative expectation gives the calculation something to answer to.

If a measured result disagrees, the disagreement is information. Perhaps the component value is different from its label, the connection is loose, or the measuring instrument changes the system. The point is to explain the difference, rather than treat the equation or the measurement as automatically correct.

## Let the diagram do some thinking

A good schematic is a way of making relationships visible. It separates the structure of the circuit from the shape of the physical wires. A careful diagram can reveal that two apparently distant points are the same electrical node, or that a complicated drawing contains a much simpler arrangement.

That habit travels beyond electronics. A software flow, a product journey, or a study plan often becomes clearer when its parts and connections are drawn. The drawing does not solve every problem. It exposes which problem needs solving first.

## Keep the explanation close

A finished answer should include more than a number. It should say what was assumed, what was predicted, what was observed, and where the model may stop being useful. That makes the work easier to check and easier to improve.

This is part of what makes electrical engineering appealing: precise reasoning stays connected to something physical. A small circuit becomes a lesson in disciplined curiosity, with room for both clear equations and honest uncertainty.

posts.title: Why I love electrical engineering and physics.
posts.subtitle: One helps me understand the world. The other gives me a way to build within it.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: I love electrical engineering and physics because they make the ordinary world feel extraordinary. A light turning on, a signal reaching a phone, or a circuit responding to an input becomes an invitation to ask how it works. The more I learn, the more I notice how much remains to be understood.
posts.body:
## The beauty of understanding

Physics gives me a language for questions that begin with curiosity. Why does a system behave this way? What stays constant, and what changes? An equation becomes more meaningful when I can connect it to a picture, a measurement, or something I can observe.

I enjoy the movement between an idea and its explanation. The answer matters, but so does the moment when separate pieces begin to fit together. That is one of the reasons I keep returning to physics: it rewards the effort to look beneath the surface.

> I want to understand the world deeply enough to build something useful in it.

## Turning ideas into something that works

Electrical engineering brings that curiosity into the practical world. A circuit is a place where an abstract model meets real components. Signals, energy, and information become things we can shape, measure, and use.

What attracts me is the balance between imagination and discipline. A design can be elegant on paper and still need adjustment when it meets reality. Understanding the difference is part of the work, and part of what makes the subject so satisfying.

## Why I study them together

As an electrical engineering and physics student at KFUPM, I do not see the two subjects as separate interests. Physics asks what is possible and why. Engineering asks how to make an idea reliable, useful, and worth building. Each gives the other a different kind of depth.

I want the habit of asking fundamental questions alongside the ability to make practical decisions. Sometimes that means moving slowly, drawing the system again, or checking an assumption I took for granted. The process is part of the appeal.

## A curiosity I want to keep

Reading gives me another way to stay curious. A good book can open a new perspective; a good scientific question can do the same. Both remind me that learning is larger than finishing a course or finding a quick answer.

I am still a student, and there is a great deal I do not know. That does not make these subjects less exciting. It gives me more reasons to continue. This blog is a place to share that curiosity: the ideas I study, the questions I keep, and the things I hope to build.

posts.title: Atomic Habits
posts.subtitle: Small actions, repeated often, become a system for change.
posts.author: James Clear
posts.intro: James Clear explains how habits form and why small improvements can matter more than occasional bursts of motivation. His argument shifts attention from ambitious goals toward the routines and surroundings that make useful actions easier to repeat.
posts.body:
## Make the next action easier

Clear organizes habit design around making a behavior obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying. The reverse approach helps weaken unwanted routines. A visible reminder, a prepared workspace, or a smaller first step can reduce the effort needed to begin.

## Think beyond motivation

The book connects repetition with identity: everyday actions provide evidence of the kind of person someone is becoming. Progress may be difficult to notice at first, so judging a routine after only a few attempts can be misleading.

## A practical reading question

Which recurring obstacle could be removed before asking for more discipline? The useful takeaway is to design one repeatable action and its setting, then observe whether the system actually helps. Small does not mean effortless, and consistency still requires adjustment.

posts.title: Educated
posts.subtitle: Education changes what we know—and how we understand home.
posts.author: Tara Westover
posts.intro: Tara Westover recounts growing up in an isolated survivalist family in Idaho without a conventional school education. Her eventual path into university opens unfamiliar intellectual possibilities while creating painful conflict with the beliefs and relationships that shaped her childhood.
posts.body:
## Learning a different language for life

Education becomes more than collecting qualifications. New historical and social perspectives allow Westover to reconsider experiences she once understood only through her family’s explanations. Knowledge changes the questions she can ask about herself.

## Belonging has a cost

The memoir examines loyalty, abuse, memory, and the difficulty of becoming independent without erasing affection for home. Academic achievement does not neatly resolve those tensions. Different people can remember the same events in incompatible ways.

## A question to carry away

What happens when learning changes the boundaries of what we can accept? The book invites reflection on the difference between respecting one’s origins and surrendering the ability to judge them. Its account remains one person’s attempt to make sense of a complicated past.

posts.title: The Midnight Library
posts.subtitle: A speculative story about regret and the lives we imagine.
posts.author: Matt Haig
posts.intro: At a moment of profound despair, Nora Seed enters a library between life and death. Each book offers a different version of her life, shaped by a decision she might have made differently. The journeys challenge her belief that one missed opportunity explains everything.
posts.body:
## The limits of an imagined perfect life

Nora explores possibilities involving careers, relationships, and ambitions. A life that looks impressive from outside can carry difficulties she never anticipated. Changing one decision does not remove uncertainty or make every other part of existence fall into place.

## Pay attention to what is already here

The story moves from comparing hypothetical achievements toward noticing connection and possibility in an imperfect present. Its emotional argument is that regret can conceal the value of ordinary relationships and future choices.

## A question to carry away

Are we comparing our real lives with complete alternatives, or only with their most attractive fragments? The novel turns that imbalance into a fantastical experiment.
posts.ending: Nora ultimately chooses to return to her original life rather than remain in an alternative. She discovers reasons to continue and approaches her future with greater openness.

posts.title: Project Hail Mary
posts.subtitle: An interstellar problem solved through experiments and friendship.
posts.author: Andy Weir
posts.intro: Ryland Grace wakes aboard a spacecraft with missing memories and dead crewmates. As he reconstructs his situation, he realizes that his mission concerns a threat to the Sun and life on Earth. Survival requires both scientific reasoning and unexpected cooperation.
posts.body:
## Turn uncertainty into an experiment

The novel repeatedly breaks an enormous problem into questions that can be measured and tested. Grace’s progress depends on revising explanations when observations disagree with them. Science becomes a practical method for acting without complete certainty.

## Cooperation across difference

An encounter with another intelligent being makes communication and mutual trust central to the mission. Differences in biology and perception become challenges to work through, rather than reasons to abandon collaboration.

## A question to carry away

When does responsibility extend beyond one’s own group? Beneath the technical puzzles, the story asks what we owe a partner who has become a friend.
posts.ending: Grace sends the solution back toward Earth but sacrifices his route home to rescue Rocky. He eventually lives on Rocky’s world, where he teaches and learns that Earth’s Sun has recovered.

posts.title: The Martian
posts.subtitle: Engineering, patience, and teamwork against an unforgiving planet.
posts.author: Andy Weir
posts.intro: After a mission emergency, astronaut Mark Watney is mistakenly left behind on Mars. With limited resources and no immediate rescue, he must keep himself alive while finding a way to communicate with Earth. The story makes survival a sequence of technical problems.
posts.body:
## Solve the problem in front of you

Watney combines botany, chemistry, repair work, and careful planning. Every solution introduces constraints of its own: energy, supplies, time, and the possibility of equipment failure. Resourcefulness means understanding those tradeoffs rather than assuming determination is enough.

## An individual effort becomes collective

The narrative expands from a solitary astronaut to the people planning his rescue. Expertise, communication, and shared responsibility become as important as his ingenuity. Humor helps Watney endure conditions it cannot change.

## A question to carry away

How can an overwhelming challenge become a manageable next step? The book offers a fictional celebration of disciplined problem solving, not a guarantee that every obstacle has an easy fix.
posts.ending: Watney reaches the departure site and launches to rendezvous with the returning Hermes crew. The final rescue succeeds through risky improvisation and coordinated effort.

posts.title: Lessons in Chemistry
posts.subtitle: A scientist refuses to let other people define her abilities.
posts.author: Bonnie Garmus
posts.intro: Elizabeth Zott is a chemist whose professional ambitions meet the sexism of 1960s America. An unexpected turn makes her a television cooking presenter. She uses that platform to explain science and challenge assumptions about what women should know and do.
posts.body:
## Who gets to be taken seriously?

The novel connects everyday prejudice with unequal access to recognition and opportunity. Elizabeth’s competence does not protect her from institutions that discount it. The tension lies between doing excellent work and being allowed to receive credit for it.

## Teach through familiar things

Cooking becomes a way to bring scientific reasoning into ordinary life. Elizabeth treats her audience as capable of understanding more than the conventions of the program expect. Knowledge can expand confidence when a teacher refuses to underestimate the learner.

## A question to carry away

What talent remains invisible because a role has already been assigned to its owner? The story pairs humor with grief, parenting, friendship, and the stubborn defense of intellectual independence.

posts.title: Where the Crawdads Sing
posts.subtitle: A marsh becomes both refuge and the setting of a mystery.
posts.author: Delia Owens
posts.intro: Kya Clark grows up largely alone in the marshes of North Carolina. The surrounding town turns her isolation into a reputation, while her close observation of the natural world becomes a source of knowledge. A suspicious death brings her life under public scrutiny.
posts.body:
## Learn to see a place closely

The marsh is more than scenery. Its patterns provide Kya with companionship, practical skills, and a language for understanding relationships. Her expertise complicates the town’s assumption that a person outside its social world must be ignorant.

## The story a community tells

A coming-of-age narrative overlaps with a murder investigation. The book asks how prejudice influences whose testimony is trusted and whose difference becomes evidence against them. Kya’s wish for connection exists alongside her reasons to distrust others.

## A question to carry away

How much do we really know about someone we have already reduced to a label? The novel makes loneliness and the desire for belonging part of its suspense.
posts.ending: Kya is acquitted of killing Chase Andrews and later shares her life with Tate. After her death, Tate discovers evidence suggesting she did kill Chase, leaving the reader to reconsider the trial and her hidden life.

posts.title: The Silent Patient
posts.subtitle: Silence, obsession, and a narrator whose account demands attention.
posts.author: Alex Michaelides
posts.intro: Alicia Berenson, a painter, stops speaking after killing her husband. Psychotherapist Theo Faber becomes determined to discover her motive. His investigation turns a seemingly straightforward crime into a mystery about memory, interpretation, and the person doing the interpreting.
posts.body:
## Absence becomes a story

Alicia’s refusal to explain herself creates a space that others fill with theories. Her artwork becomes another possible form of testimony. The novel asks how easily an observer can mistake a compelling interpretation for established truth.

## Question the investigator

Theo’s personal history and intense interest in Alicia matter to the narrative. Following his account means watching not only what he discovers but also how he directs the reader’s attention. Apparent insight can hide a desire to control the story.

## A question to carry away

What evidence do we overlook when we trust the person arranging it for us? The thriller’s force comes from the distance between an explanation and the motives behind it.
posts.ending: Theo was the intruder who confronted Alicia and Gabriel before the killing. The narrative has concealed the timing of his actions. Alicia’s written account ultimately exposes his involvement.

posts.title: The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo
posts.subtitle: A public legend tells a private story of love and ambition.
posts.author: Taylor Jenkins Reid
posts.intro: Retired film star Evelyn Hugo chooses journalist Monique Grant to record her life. The seven marriages that shaped Evelyn’s public image frame a much less orderly private history. Monique gradually discovers that the interview is not simply an opportunity to write a celebrity biography.
posts.body:
## A life larger than its headlines

Evelyn describes the bargains and performances that helped her survive Hollywood. Marriage can be a relationship, a shield, or a career decision. The novel separates the story an industry sells from the needs of the person living inside it.

## Ambition does not cancel vulnerability

Love, friendship, sexuality, grief, and self-protection complicate Evelyn’s carefully maintained persona. Her choices can be understandable without being harmless. The book resists making either success or suffering a complete explanation of character.

## A question to carry away

Who controls the final account of a life? Monique must decide what to do with a story that gives her power while changing her understanding of its teller.

posts.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
posts.subtitle: The mental shortcuts behind judgments that feel obvious.
posts.author: Daniel Kahneman
posts.intro: Daniel Kahneman examines how people judge, predict, and choose. He describes fast, automatic thinking alongside slower, effortful reasoning. These are useful models of mental activity, not two neatly separated organs or personalities.
posts.body:
## Confidence is not the same as accuracy

A coherent explanation can feel convincing even when the evidence is limited. The book explores anchoring, framing, and the tendency to neglect statistical information. Intuition works well in some settings but becomes unreliable when patterns are misleading or feedback is poor.

## Evaluate the decision, not only the result

Luck can produce a good outcome from a weak choice. Kahneman’s work encourages attention to the information available at the time and to how comparisons shape preference. Slower thinking helps, but it is not automatically free of bias.

## A question to carry away

What would change this judgment, and what relevant information is missing? The useful habit is to make reasoning more inspectable rather than assume that knowing a bias makes us immune to it.

posts.title: Outlive
posts.subtitle: A framework for thinking about longer, healthier lives.
posts.author: Peter Attia with Bill Gifford
posts.intro: Peter Attia argues that longevity should include preserving physical, cognitive, and emotional capacity, not simply adding years. With Bill Gifford, he presents a prevention-focused approach to chronic disease and the decisions that may influence later life.
posts.body:
## Look ahead before a crisis

The book contrasts reacting to illness with considering risk earlier. It discusses exercise, nutrition, sleep, and emotional wellbeing as interacting parts of a long-term strategy. Attia’s framework emphasizes individual circumstances rather than a single universal routine.

## Ask what the extra years are for

Healthspan gives the argument its practical meaning: the ability to continue doing things that matter. The book connects future ambitions with present preparation, while recognizing that physical performance is not a substitute for relationships or emotional health.

## A question to carry away

What abilities would make later life meaningful? This is a summary of the author’s perspective, not a personalized treatment or testing plan. Specific medical decisions require appropriate clinical advice and current evidence.

posts.title: Becoming
posts.subtitle: A life shaped by education, public service, and changing expectations.
posts.author: Michelle Obama
posts.intro: Michelle Obama recounts her childhood in Chicago, education, professional choices, family life, and years in the White House. The memoir examines the gap between an individual’s developing identity and the expectations attached to increasingly visible roles.
posts.body:
## Success does not settle every question

The narrative follows choices about work, relationships, and service rather than treating achievement as a final destination. A path that appears impressive can still require reconsideration when its daily demands no longer fit someone’s values.

## The person inside the public role

Family relationships and ordinary concerns continue alongside political responsibility. Public attention changes how a life is interpreted, often reducing complexity to an image. The memoir restores some of that complexity through the author’s own account.

## A question to carry away

Which ambitions are chosen, and which are inherited from other people’s expectations? The idea of becoming keeps identity open to development rather than defining a person by one title or period of life.

posts.title: Born a Crime
posts.subtitle: Language, belonging, and a childhood shaped by apartheid.
posts.author: Trevor Noah
posts.intro: Trevor Noah tells stories of growing up in South Africa during apartheid and its aftermath. His birth to a Black mother and white father violated the racial order of the time. Humor shares space with poverty, exclusion, violence, and his mother’s determination.
posts.body:
## Language can open a door

Moving between languages helps Noah navigate communities that classify him differently. Speaking to people in their own language becomes a way to connect across boundaries, even when those boundaries have been enforced by institutions and custom.

## The relationship at the center

His mother’s resourcefulness and independence give the memoir its emotional structure. Her choices expose both the possibilities of refusing assigned limits and the danger of living within violent conditions. The comedy does not erase those stakes.

## A question to carry away

How do laws and social labels shape experiences that appear purely personal? The memoir makes a historical system understandable through everyday situations without turning one childhood into every South African’s story.

posts.title: Shoe Dog
posts.subtitle: The uncertain early years behind a globally familiar brand.
posts.author: Phil Knight
posts.intro: Phil Knight recounts the early development of the company that became Nike. Starting with the idea of importing running shoes, he describes a business built through relationships, financial pressure, experimentation, and a team whose work preceded its eventual fame.
posts.body:
## The outcome hides the uncertainty

Looking backward can make a successful company seem inevitable. Knight’s account instead emphasizes recurring constraints and decisions made without a secure view of the future. Growth creates new problems as well as new opportunities.

## A company is also a group of people

The memoir connects the enterprise with the personalities and commitments of its early collaborators. Shared purpose matters, but does not remove conflict, operational demands, or the difficulty of sustaining the business.

## A question to carry away

Which part of a success story disappears when it becomes a brand legend? This is a founder’s retrospective perspective, so it is most useful as a view into decisions and experience rather than a formula that guarantees another venture’s success.

posts.title: The Creative Act: A Way of Being
posts.subtitle: Creativity begins with attention before it becomes a finished object.
posts.author: Rick Rubin
posts.intro: Rick Rubin presents creativity as a way of noticing and responding to the world. Rather than a technical guide to music production, the book offers short reflections on the conditions that make discovery, experimentation, and artistic judgment possible.
posts.body:
## Collect before you decide

An artist needs material to work with: observations, sounds, ideas, and experiences. Rubin encourages openness before selection. Judging an idea too early can prevent it from becoming something that could not yet be imagined.

## Experiment without surrendering craft

Making work involves both exploration and decisions about what belongs. The creative process requires room for alternatives, but eventually an artist must shape and release something. A productive constraint can focus attention without becoming a permanent rule.

## A question to carry away

What changes when a drawing session begins with curiosity rather than the demand to prove talent? The book’s suggestions are invitations to test a creative practice, not scientific laws or one mandatory method.

posts.title: The Anxious Generation
posts.subtitle: An argument about childhood, smartphones, and shared responsibility.
posts.author: Jonathan Haidt
posts.intro: Jonathan Haidt argues that the shift toward smartphone-centered childhood has contributed to worsening adolescent mental health. He connects digital life with reduced independent play and proposes changes that families, schools, and communities could make together.
posts.body:
## An environment, not only an individual habit

The book examines how constant connection can reshape attention, social comparison, and everyday relationships. Haidt contrasts exposure to online risks with restrictions on ordinary offline independence. The focus is on a broader social environment rather than blaming individual children.

## Change is easier when it is shared

Proposed responses include delaying smartphone and social-media use, phone-free schools, and more opportunities for independent activity. The argument emphasizes coordinated norms because one family’s choices are affected by what surrounding peers do.

## A question to carry away

Which digital expectations have become normal without a deliberate decision? The book presents a particular causal argument; interpretation of the evidence remains debated. Its claims should be evaluated rather than treated as a complete explanation of every young person’s experience.

posts.title: Brief Answers to the Big Questions
posts.subtitle: Scientific curiosity reaches from the cosmos to humanity’s future.
posts.author: Stephen Hawking
posts.intro: Stephen Hawking considers large questions about the universe, intelligent life, technology, and human survival. The collection combines scientific explanation with his perspective on the responsibilities that come with knowledge and the uncertainties that remain.
posts.body:
## A question can be bigger than its present answer

The essays approach subjects such as the origins of the universe and black holes through scientific reasoning. They communicate a willingness to ask fundamental questions without pretending that every aspect of reality has been settled.

## Progress creates responsibility

Hawking also looks toward artificial intelligence, exploration, and risks to humanity’s future. These discussions extend beyond established physical theory into forecasting and judgment. Distinguishing those kinds of claims helps a reader stay curious and critical.

## A question to carry away

How should an expanding ability to understand and build change our sense of responsibility? The lasting invitation is to keep asking difficult questions while remembering that an accessible explanation is a beginning, not the end of a scientific education.

posts.title: Dare to Lead
posts.subtitle: Leadership requires the courage to face uncertainty together.
posts.author: Brené Brown
posts.intro: Brené Brown connects leadership with developing people and ideas rather than accumulating status. Her approach emphasizes vulnerability, clear values, trust, and the ability to recover after failure. Courage is presented as a practice that can be developed.
posts.body:
## Replace the performance of certainty

A leader does not need to pretend to have every answer. Asking better questions and admitting uncertainty can make difficult work more honest. This openness does not remove accountability; it makes the real problem easier for a team to discuss.

## Make values visible in behavior

The book asks teams to connect stated principles with everyday decisions and conversations. Trust depends on repeated conduct, not merely a declaration that people should feel safe. Avoiding discomfort can allow unresolved issues to grow.

## A question to carry away

What conversation is being postponed because it might feel uncomfortable? The useful test is whether a leadership habit helps people do clearer, more responsible work together—not whether it gives the leader a convincing image.

posts.title: Digital Minimalism
posts.subtitle: Choose digital tools according to the life you want them to support.
posts.author: Cal Newport
posts.intro: Cal Newport proposes a deliberate approach to personal technology. Instead of keeping every tool that offers some benefit, digital minimalism asks which tools strongly support chosen values and under what conditions they should be used.
posts.body:
## Begin with a reason, not an app

The argument shifts attention from scattered settings changes toward a philosophy of use. A tool can be useful while still occupying more time or attention than its contribution deserves. Convenience alone does not decide its place.

## Create room for something better

Newport describes a thirty-day break from optional technologies followed by selective reintroduction. Meaningful leisure, solitude, and direct conversation matter because removing a habit leaves a space that another activity needs to fill.

## A question to carry away

Which online activity has a clear purpose, and which has become the default whenever there is a pause? The goal is not to reject technology but to make its role specific enough that it serves the rest of life.

posts.title: Factfulness
posts.subtitle: A clearer view of the world starts with questioning our instincts.
posts.author: Hans Rosling, Ola Rosling & Anna Rosling Rönnlund
posts.intro: The Roslings examine why people often misunderstand global conditions and trends. They describe habits of thought that make dramatic events, simple divisions, and alarming stories feel more representative than the wider evidence supports.
posts.body:
## Look for the missing comparison

A number becomes more meaningful when its scale and context are visible. The book encourages comparisons, attention to change over time, and skepticism toward descriptions that divide a varied world into only two categories.

## Improvement and suffering can coexist

Recognizing progress does not require denying serious problems. The authors argue that a more accurate picture helps people direct concern toward the right questions. Optimism is less useful than a habit of checking what the evidence actually shows.

## A question to carry away

What would a less dramatic but more complete account look like? Published statistics belong to their period, so specific figures should be updated before reuse. The enduring lesson is a way of examining claims, not a promise that every trend is positive.

posts.title: For my dad, Laqman.
posts.subtitle: A little space for a love that means more than I can put into words.
posts.author: Ahmad Alabbas
posts.intro: This blog holds many of the things I love: books, drawing, electrical engineering, and physics. But it would not feel like my own space without a place for my dad, Laqman. Dad, I love you. I want those words to be here, plainly and sincerely.
posts.body:
## More than a name on a page

A photograph can show a face. A name can introduce a person. Neither can quite explain what my dad means to me. That is why I wanted to write this note: to give a little room to a feeling that matters deeply to me.

I do not need a special occasion to say that I love him. Sometimes the simplest words are the ones most worth saying. This is one of those times.

> Dad, I love you. I want those words to have a place here.

## Love deserves to be said

I spend a lot of time thinking about ideas and how to express them clearly. Writing about love is different. There is no formula that makes the words complete, and no perfect sentence that can hold everything I feel.

Still, I want to try. I want my dad to know that he matters to me, that I am proud to call him my dad, and that my love for him belongs among the things I choose to share.

## The person I hope to become

I have things I want to learn, projects I want to build, and a future I am still discovering. Alongside those ambitions is a quieter wish: to be a son who shows his love through attention, care, and the way he treats the people closest to him.

A public note is only one small expression of that wish. I want the feeling behind these words to carry into ordinary days too: making time, listening, and remembering to say what matters.

## For you, Dad

Laqman, this page is for you. Not because a website can measure love, but because I wanted a corner of mine to say something personal and true.

I love you, Dad. As I keep learning, drawing, reading, and building, I want these words to stay here: a simple reminder of someone who means so much to me.

settings.hero_intro: I’m Ahmad. I read, draw, study electrical engineering and physics, and build things that might make life a little better.
settings.about_title: A reader, a builder, always a student.
settings.about_body:
I’m Ahmad Alabbas, from Saudi Arabia. I study electrical engineering and physics at KFUPM.

## A notebook for the work

I love reading and drawing. Books give me a way to explore unfamiliar ideas, question what I know, and see things from another perspective. Science offers a way to understand the world. Engineering offers a way to make something work.

## Beyond the desk

Books, travel, and learning languages offer other ways to see familiar things differently.

## What you’ll find here

Book summaries, articles on science and building, and a gallery of photographs from my December 2025 London trip.
settings.work_body:
## Veelad

A print-on-demand marketplace project, connecting independent design with everyday products.

## Ausket

Exploring how a website builder can make publishing clear and approachable.

## ALABBAS

Entrepreneurial work, ideas, and lessons from building over time.
